subtitle: Unreal conditions, now and then, and als ob
words.intro: Dostoevsky lost everything at the tables in Wiesbaden. Today the casino still has the chandeliers and a dress code, and anybody may go and find out what they would have done with the money.

grammar[0].fact: Germans love a good lottery fantasy: *Wenn ich im Lotto gewinne, …* is a staple of office conversation. The chance of the top prize in *6 aus 49* is about one in 140 million. Every Saturday evening, millions of people choose to find this out.

grammar[1].fact: *Tu nicht so, als ob!* Don’t pretend! A parent’s sentence, with no ending needed. *Als ob!* alone is a teenager’s: yeah, right. The grammar is not simple, but the shrug is the same as anywhere.

document.intro: A real notice in a modern German casino. Regular guests can sign in with the veins of their hand. It’s very short, with three commands. And there’s a ladybird.
document.fact: German casinos must by law check who comes in, because players can have themselves barred. The ladybird, *der Marienkäfer*, is a German lucky charm, so it has come to the right place.
reading.intro: Maya has won a voucher for an evening at the casino in Wiesbaden. She has taken Frau Huber, who has dressed as if she owned it. Each has fifty euros. A man at the table is explaining his system to anyone who stands still.
reading.photos[0].caption: Der Tisch: Wenn du jetzt auf die Sieben gesetzt hättest …
reading.fact: Germany has dozens of state-licensed casinos, and Wiesbaden’s goes back to the 1770s. Dostoevsky’s novel *The Gambler* came out of his time at German tables. Gambling law is strict: you need an ID, and you can have yourself barred, and casinos must check the list.
